Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally
Protect society, the common good, public trust and the infrastructure
explanation: The ISC2 canons are ordered: (1) protect society, the common good, the necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure; (2) act honorably; (3) provide diligent service; (4) advance the profession. web_sources.title: DestCert: Unraveling CISSP Domain 1 — Security and Risk Management

web_sources.title: ThreatOnTheWire: Ownership of Information and Assets

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

explanation: Scoping removes irrelevant controls from a baseline. Tailoring then modifies the remaining controls to fit operational reality (e.g., parameter selection). Baselining is selecting a starting catalog. Compensating is replacing one control with another that achieves the objective.

Documenting an organization-defined frequency for the control
explanation: Removing a control from the baseline is scoping — not tailoring. Tailoring activities (per NIST 800-53B) include parameter selection, compensating controls, and organisation-defined values. The exam tests this scoping-vs-tailoring distinction directly.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Scoping & Tailoring Security Controls

The format of the data (paper vs digital)

PHI is a subset of PII covered specifically under HIPAA in healthcare contexts
PII is only digital; PHI is only paper
explanation: PHI is the HIPAA-defined subset of PII connected to health information held by covered entities and business associates. PII is the broader category. The exam tests subset-vs-superset framing and which regulation governs each.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

stem: Which phase of the data lifecycle is MOST often overlooked, leading to data accumulation beyond useful life?
explanation: Organisations are good at creating, storing, and using data; archive and destroy phases (and the policy/automation around them) are habitually neglected — leading to accumulation, e-discovery cost, and breach exposure. The CISSP exam emphasises end-of-life discipline.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

stem: Confidential computing primarily addresses the protection of data in which state?
explanation: Confidential computing (Intel SGX, AMD SEV, ARM TrustZone, AWS Nitro Enclaves) protects data while it is being processed in memory — the historically weakest of the three states. Encryption at rest and TLS already address rest and transit.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

stem: Degaussing is MOST appropriate for which media?
choices: Magnetic media such as HDDs and tapes
explanation: Degaussing reorders magnetic domains to a random state — it works on magnetic HDDs and tapes. SSDs and flash store data in NAND cells (no magnetic field), and optical media use pits/lands. Modern hybrid drives also need crypto-erase or physical destruction.

stem: Which technique transforms PII into a non-sensitive surrogate value that can be used for analytics while preserving referential integrity but NOT reversibility without a vault lookup?
explanation: Tokenisation substitutes sensitive values with surrogate tokens, with reversibility only via a secure token vault. Encryption is mathematically reversible with the key. Hashing is one-way. Anonymisation aims to be irreversible, removing identifiability entirely.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

stem: Which technique aggregates and modifies data so that individual data subjects cannot be re-identified, even with auxiliary information?
explanation: Anonymisation aims for irreversibility against re-identification (k-anonymity, differential privacy). Pseudonymisation replaces identifiers with placeholders that CAN be relinked with a key — it is reversible and remains personal data under GDPR. Tokenisation and encryption are reversible.

Degauss in compliance with NIST 800-88 purge guidance and verify
Store indefinitely in case of legal hold
explanation: For magnetic tape with high-impact data, NIST 800-88 purge via degaussing followed by verification is appropriate (or destroy if leaving control). Quick format is not sanitisation. Indefinite storage violates retention policy. Encrypting then discarding leaves the keyed ciphertext recoverable if the key leaks.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev 1: Guidelines for Media Sanitization

explanation: US federal classification: Confidential = damage; Secret = serious damage; Top Secret = exceptionally grave damage. FOUO is a control marking, not a classification. CISSP frequently tests these tiers and their commercial equivalents.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

choices: Easier user understanding and consistent application of controls
explanation: Excessive tiers confuse users and lead to inconsistent classification decisions. Three to four levels is generally optimal — enough to differentiate, not so many that users default to a single label. The other choices are not the primary driver.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

Lack of feature parity with current versions
explanation: EOS means the vendor stops releasing security patches; newly disclosed vulnerabilities remain exploitable. Warranty, fees, and features are concerns but secondary to security exposure. Manager-mindset answers focus on residual risk.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

Automated asset-discovery tooling integrated with CMDB and feedback to the configuration baseline
explanation: Automated discovery tied to a CMDB (with reconciliation to the configuration baseline) is the only scalable, accurate approach for modern environments. Manual approaches drift quickly and miss ephemeral assets like containers/VMs. The exam favours automation + CMDB.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

stem: An organisation collects email addresses for marketing. A user requests deletion under GDPR. The organisation MUST:

Comply within one month unless a specified GDPR exemption applies
Charge a reasonable fee for processing the request
Wait for legal counsel to review every individual request
explanation: Article 17 'right to erasure' obliges controllers to delete without undue delay (and within one month for response per Article 12). Limited exemptions exist (legal claims, freedom of expression). Fees and per-request legal review violate the spirit of the regulation.

web_sources.title: GDPR Info: General Data Protection Regulation full text

explanation: Pattern matching with structural validation (Luhn for PAN, SSN format, IBAN check digits) catches data wherever it lives, including inside Word docs and email bodies. File-type or keyword approaches generate excessive false positives or miss data. Training is necessary but is not a DLP technique.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

choices: Integrated classification dialog (e.g., labelling at save) plus DLP enforcement
explanation: Integrating labelling into the user workflow (Microsoft Information Protection, Google Drive labels) and enforcing with DLP gives consistent classification at creation, with downstream control choices following. The other approaches are either after-the-fact or one-size-fits-all.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

explanation: For SEDs, NIST 800-88 specifies cryptographic erase (destroy/replace the MEK) often combined with the drive's ATA Secure Erase. Multi-pass overwrites are unreliable on SSDs due to wear levelling. Degaussing does not work on flash. The DoD 5220 standard was retired for modern drives.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev 1: Guidelines for Media Sanitization
InventiveHQ: NIST 800-88 — Clear, Purge, Destroy Methods Explained

explanation: NIST 800-53 is the controls catalog (Rev 5 integrates security + privacy). 800-37 is the RMF process; 800-30 is risk assessment; 800-115 is technical security testing. Memorising the 800-series numbers is high-yield exam prep.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: Security and Privacy Controls

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-60 Vol I Rev 1: Mapping Information Types to Security Categories

Apply for a data export license
explanation: GDPR Chapter V restricts transfers; before transferring, the controller must rely on a transfer mechanism — Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs), an adequacy decision, Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs), or specific derogations. The other choices are not the legal prerequisite.

choices: Sanitize per data classification, then dispose with documentation
explanation: Sanitisation (Clear/Purge/Destroy per classification) MUST precede disposal/reassignment/donation. Documentation (chain of custody, certificate of destruction) provides audit evidence. Discarding without sanitisation is a data-leakage event waiting to happen.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

Demote the entire data set to Public
Force the security team to re-classify everything
explanation: Default-confidential is a common failure mode that erodes the value of classification. Improving training, adjusting defaults, and possibly adding intermediate tiers restores meaningful differentiation. Eliminating the tier or wholesale re-classification overcorrects.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

explanation: GDPR Article 15 grants data subjects the right to access their personal data — controllers must respond (typically within one month) with a copy and information about processing. The other choices are unrelated to the SAR concept.

web_sources.title: GDPR Info: General Data Protection Regulation full text

explanation: Markings tell users (and downstream automation) what controls apply — encryption, courier method, sanitisation requirement. Without consistent marking, classification cannot translate into action. Inventory and warranty are operational concerns.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

choices: The minimum acceptable security posture for a class of systems
The list of all CVEs affecting an asset
The encryption standard for data at rest
explanation: A baseline is the minimum acceptable configuration for a given system class — for instance, a Windows server hardening baseline. It is the starting point that scoping/tailoring then refines. The other choices are different artefacts.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

choices: A documented lawful basis (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interest, public task, or legitimate interest)
explanation: Article 6 enumerates six lawful bases — collection without one is unlawful. Convenience and vendor recommendations are not bases. Storage capacity is unrelated. Knowing the six bases is critical for the exam.

web_sources.title: GDPR Info: General Data Protection Regulation full text

stem: An organisation that needs to retire a multi-function copier with on-board storage MUST FIRST:
choices: Donate the copier to a school
Sanitize the on-board storage per NIST 800-88 before transfer
Sell the copier to recover residual value
Power off the device for 30 days
explanation: Multi-function devices retain scanned/printed documents on internal storage and are routinely overlooked in disposal. Sanitisation MUST precede disposal/donation/sale. Powering off does not erase storage.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev 1: Guidelines for Media Sanitization

choices: The data is older than 10 years
The original sensitivity has lapsed and continued classification offers no protective benefit
explanation: Declassification is appropriate when the underlying sensitivity has lapsed (e.g., a quarterly result becomes public after the earnings release). Pure age is not a sufficient criterion; storage costs and personnel turnover are not classification drivers.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Asset Security in CISSP Domain 2

stem: Which security model enforces 'no read up, no write down' to preserve confidentiality?
explanation: Bell-LaPadula is the canonical confidentiality model. 'No read up' (simple security property) prevents reading higher-classified data; '*-property' (no write down) prevents leaking high-classified data into low-classified objects. Biba is the integrity inverse. Clark-Wilson focuses on transactional integrity. Brewer-Nash addresses conflict-of-interest.

stem: Which security model preserves integrity using 'no read down, no write up'?
explanation: Biba is the integrity inverse of Bell-LaPadula: 'no read down' avoids contamination by lower-integrity data; 'no write up' prevents low-integrity subjects from corrupting high-integrity objects. Lattice is a generalisation; Take-Grant analyses rights propagation; Bell-LaPadula is confidentiality.

web_sources.title: SIIT: CISSP Security Models in Exams

stem: Which security model enforces well-formed transactions and separation of duty between unconstrained data items, transformation procedures, and constrained data items?
explanation: Clark-Wilson focuses on transactional integrity in commercial environments using TPs (transformation procedures), CDIs/UDIs (constrained/unconstrained data items), and IVPs. Bell-LaPadula is confidentiality; Biba is simpler integrity; Goguen-Meseguer is non-interference.

web_sources.title: SIIT: CISSP Security Models in Exams

stem: Which model is used to prevent conflict of interest in data access (e.g., a consultant cannot access two competing clients' data)?
explanation: Brewer-Nash, also called Chinese Wall, dynamically restricts access based on prior accesses to prevent conflict of interest. The other models address confidentiality, rights propagation analysis, or rights creation/deletion semantics — not conflict-of-interest enforcement.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which property does a cryptographic hash function FUNDAMENTALLY provide?
explanation: A hash provides integrity: any change to the input changes the digest. Confidentiality requires encryption. Non-repudiation needs hashing PLUS asymmetric signatures (a hash alone proves nothing about origin). Forward secrecy is a property of key-exchange protocols.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which AES mode provides both confidentiality AND integrity in a single primitive?
explanation: AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) is an authenticated encryption mode — it produces ciphertext and an authentication tag in one pass. ECB is insecure (deterministic). CBC and CTR provide confidentiality only and require a separate MAC for integrity. TLS 1.3 mandates AEAD modes like GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Types of Ciphers — ECB, CBC, OFB & More
ITKnowledgeBases: Block Cipher Modes Explained — CISSP Guide

stem: Which AES mode should NEVER be used for general-purpose encryption due to producing identical ciphertext for identical plaintext blocks?
explanation: ECB (Electronic Codebook) is deterministic — equal plaintext blocks yield equal ciphertext, leaking patterns (the 'Tux penguin' image is the classic demonstration). CBC, CTR, GCM all use IVs/nonces to randomise. ECB is acceptable only for encrypting random short data like keys.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Types of Ciphers — ECB, CBC, OFB & More

stem: Which property does a digital signature on a message provide that a MAC does NOT?
explanation: A digital signature uses asymmetric cryptography — only the holder of the private key can produce it, providing non-repudiation. A MAC uses a shared symmetric secret, so any holder of the key could have produced it (no non-repudiation). Both can provide integrity and authenticity in their respective trust models.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which asymmetric algorithm relies on the difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves to provide equivalent security to RSA at smaller key sizes?
explanation: ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) provides RSA-equivalent security at much smaller keys (e.g., 256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA). Diffie-Hellman uses discrete logs in a finite field. DSA is a signature algorithm. RSA factors large composites. ECC's compactness makes it ideal for IoT and TLS.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which is the BEST description of a Hardware Security Module (HSM)?
choices: A cryptographic library installed on every server
A tamper-resistant hardware appliance for key generation, storage, and crypto operations
A backup mechanism for shared secrets
explanation: An HSM is a dedicated, tamper-resistant device that performs key lifecycle and crypto operations without exposing keys outside its boundary. Many are FIPS 140-2/3 validated. Choices A and C are cryptographic concepts but not HSMs; choice D is a different hardware category (SED).

web_sources.title: wolfSSL: Difference between HSM, TPM, Secure Enclave, Secure Element

stem: A TPM (Trusted Platform Module) is BEST described as:
choices: A standalone HSM appliance for the data center
A chip on the motherboard providing platform integrity and a hardware root of trust
A network-attached device for high-volume crypto
A software emulation of an HSM
explanation: A TPM is a passive chip embedded on the platform that supports measured boot, sealed storage, and remote attestation — a hardware root of trust at the device level. HSMs are standalone or PCIe and target high-volume crypto operations. TPM-Fail and similar research show TPMs can have side-channel weaknesses.

stem: An organisation must protect data confidentiality from a future quantum-capable adversary that may harvest ciphertext today and break it later. Which mitigation is MOST APPROPRIATE today?
choices: Adopt AES-256 for symmetric encryption (Grover halves brute-force strength) and plan for hybrid post-quantum KEM (e.g., ML-KEM/Kyber) for asymmetric
Stop encrypting data because it will all be broken anyway
explanation: Symmetric AES-256 retains roughly 128-bit security against Grover's algorithm — sufficient for long-lived data. Asymmetric algorithms (RSA/ECC) fall to Shor's algorithm and need migration. NIST finalised ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (204), SLH-DSA (205) in 2024. RSA-4096 alone does not survive Shor; MD5 is broken. Hybrid (classical + PQ) is the recommended migration path.

explanation: EAL describes evaluation rigor (EAL1 functionally tested → EAL7 formally verified design and tested). It does NOT mean the product is more secure in absolute terms — an EAL4 product can be more secure than an EAL6 product evaluated against weaker functionality. Cryptographic strength is a separate property captured in the Security Target.

web_sources.title: Common Criteria Portal

stem: Which standard validates cryptographic modules and is required for US federal cryptographic deployments?
explanation: FIPS 140-3 (the successor to 140-2) validates cryptographic modules at four levels (1-4). FIPS 199 is security categorisation. CC EAL is general-purpose evaluation. ISO 27001 is ISMS. FIPS 140-3 incorporates ISO/IEC 19790:2012.

Two processes communicating by modulating delays in shared resource access
explanation: A covert timing channel signals information by varying the timing of resource access (CPU, disk, network). The other choices describe overt or unrelated channels. Covert STORAGE channels modulate stored values; covert TIMING channels modulate timing. Both are unintended disclosure paths.

choices: Designing the environment to reduce criminal opportunity through territoriality, surveillance, and access control
explanation: CPTED uses environmental cues (sight lines, lighting, landscaping, signage, layout) to deter crime. Headcount, camera reduction, and insurance are tangential. The three CPTED strategies often tested are natural surveillance, natural access control, and territorial reinforcement.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which datacenter HVAC consideration is MOST critical for equipment longevity?
choices: Maintained temperature and humidity within manufacturer specifications
explanation: Heat and humidity drift are the dominant electronic failure causes — datacenters target ~64-81°F (18-27°C) and 40-60% relative humidity per ASHRAE TC 9.9. Excess humidity → corrosion; low humidity → ESD. Aesthetics and lighting are not equipment factors.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which is the BEST description of perfect forward secrecy (PFS)?

Compromise of long-term private keys does not allow decryption of past session traffic
All sessions use the same ephemeral key
Each user has a unique permanent key
explanation: PFS uses ephemeral session keys (DHE/ECDHE) that are not derivable from long-term keys, so capturing long-term keys later does not retroactively decrypt past sessions. TLS 1.3 mandates PFS by removing RSA key transport. Choices A, C, D contradict the property.

stem: Which mechanism BEST establishes that a public key actually belongs to its claimed owner in a PKI?
choices: X.509 certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority
explanation: X.509 certificates issued by trusted CAs bind a public key to an identity through the CA's verification + signature. Self-signed certificates lack third-party validation. DNS TXT records can support verification (DANE, ACME) but are not the binding mechanism. Email is too weak.

stem: Which mechanism is the FASTEST to revoke a compromised certificate in real-time?
choices: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) with stapling
Manual phone call to relying parties
explanation: OCSP returns near-real-time status; OCSP stapling has the server attach a fresh signed response, avoiding client-side OCSP requests. CRLs are typically published periodically and may be hours/days stale. Calls and DNS TTL are not certificate-revocation mechanisms.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which is the PRIMARY purpose of key escrow?
choices: Allow the vendor to monitor traffic
Provide an authorised third party access to keys under defined conditions (e.g., legal subpoena, employee termination)
explanation: Key escrow stores keys with a trusted third party for retrieval under defined conditions. It is controversial because it weakens guarantee of sole possession but is sometimes required by regulation or operationally for ediscovery. The other choices misdescribe escrow.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5: Recommendation for Key Management
DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a Trusted Computing Base (TCB)?
choices: The set of components within a system whose correct operation is essential to enforcing the security policy
explanation: The TCB is the set of hardware, software, and firmware whose correctness is essential to enforcing the security policy. Reducing the TCB reduces attack surface — a key principle in formal models. The other choices are unrelated.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which is NOT a property of a reference monitor?
choices: Small enough to be analysed and tested
explanation: Reference monitor properties (the 'NEAT' / 'always invoked + tamper-proof + verifiable' triad): always invoked, tamper-proof, and small/verifiable. User-runtime modification would defeat the security guarantee. The OS kernel implements the reference monitor concept.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: A 'birthday attack' is MOST relevant to which cryptographic primitive?
explanation: Birthday paradox attacks search for collisions in hash functions — the expected effort to find a collision is roughly 2^(n/2) for an n-bit hash. SHA-1 (160 bits → ~2^80) is consequently considered weak; SHA-256 (~2^128) remains strong. The other choices are not the canonical target.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which attack pattern relies on the attacker observing how a system reacts to malformed padding to recover plaintext?
explanation: Padding oracle attacks (POODLE in SSL3, BEAST adjacent issues, AES-CBC mishandling) decrypt by submitting modified ciphertext and observing whether the server accepts or rejects. Authenticated encryption (GCM) prevents this. Replay reuses; brute force tries every key; differential analyses chosen-plaintext distributions.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which protocol provides authenticated key exchange suitable for resisting man-in-the-middle attacks during ephemeral session establishment?
choices: Authenticated DHE / ECDHE with certificate-based identity
explanation: Plain DH/ECDHE provides forward secrecy but is unauthenticated alone — it must be combined with certificate-based identity (TLS_ECDHE_*_*_GCM_*) to resist MITM. Anonymous DH is vulnerable. MD5 is broken. Static RSA key transport gives no PFS and is removed from TLS 1.3.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which secure-design principle says a system should DEFAULT to denying access when an explicit allow is missing?
explanation: Fail-safe defaults (a Saltzer & Schroeder principle) says deny by default; access is granted only by explicit allow. Open design says security should not depend on obscurity. Economy of mechanism keeps designs simple. Complete mediation requires every access to be checked.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which secure-design principle says EVERY access to EVERY object must be checked for authority?
explanation: Complete mediation requires every access (not just first access) be checked — caching access decisions can violate it (TOCTOU class issues). Least privilege limits rights. Open design avoids security-by-obscurity. Defense in depth layers controls.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: What is the GREATEST security challenge introduced by IoT devices in an enterprise?
choices: Long lifespans, infrequent patching, weak default credentials, and lateral-movement potential
explanation: IoT devices typically combine outdated firmware, default creds, exposed management interfaces, and 5-10+ year lifespans — they become persistent footholds (Mirai-class botnets). Mitigations include segmentation, MFA where supported, vendor SBOM review, and lifecycle planning.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Under the cloud shared responsibility model, who is typically responsible for the GUEST OS patches in an IaaS deployment?
explanation: In IaaS, the customer manages from the guest OS upward (OS, runtimes, applications, data). The provider handles physical, network, hypervisor. PaaS shifts more to the provider; SaaS shifts almost everything except identity/data classification. Knowing the responsibility split per service model is exam-critical.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which is the PRIMARY security risk introduced by hypervisor 'VM escape' vulnerabilities?
choices: A guest VM can break out of isolation and compromise the host or other guests
explanation: VM escape breaks the hypervisor's isolation guarantee, allowing one guest to access the host or other guests — catastrophic in multi-tenant clouds. Mitigation includes hypervisor patching, minimal attack surface (Type 1 hypervisors), and tenant isolation policies.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: What is 'process isolation' designed to ensure?
choices: Each process operates in its own protected memory space, unable to read or modify others
explanation: Process isolation prevents one process from interfering with another's memory or state — implemented via virtual memory, MMU enforcement, and OS access controls. Without it, a single bug or malware could cascade. Choices A, C, D are unrelated to isolation.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which technique randomises memory addresses to make exploitation of memory corruption more difficult?
explanation: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomisation) randomises base addresses of code/heap/stack/libraries. DEP marks data pages non-executable. NX is the hardware bit DEP uses. SMEP prevents kernel from executing user-space pages. CISSP often pairs ASLR + DEP/NX as standard defences.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide
DestCert: Vulnerabilities in Systems MindMap — Domain 3

stem: Which lock type provides the HIGHEST level of resistance to physical attack and is GENERALLY required for high-classification facilities?
explanation: For high-security entry, layered controls (mantrap + biometric + supervisor approval) provide the strongest assurance. Pin tumblers are easily picked or bumped. Combination locks vary in quality. The answer reflects defense-in-depth: a single technology rarely suffices for high-classification rooms.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which trust model is implemented when a CA at the top of a hierarchy issues subordinate-CA certificates that issue end-entity certificates?
explanation: Hierarchical (root → subordinate → end-entity) is the standard PKI structure (e.g., public web PKI). Web of trust (PGP) is peer-based. Cross-certification establishes pairwise trust. Bridge CA connects multiple PKIs through a central node.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which property is required of a hash function for use in digital signatures?
explanation: Hash functions for signatures must be collision-resistant (two different inputs producing the same digest would let an attacker forge a signature). They are deliberately one-way (irreversible), keyless (unlike MACs), and produce fixed-length output.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which symmetric algorithm is the CURRENT US federal standard for encrypting classified information?
explanation: AES is FIPS 197, replacing DES. 3DES is deprecated by NIST since 2023 (SP 800-131A Rev 3). DES has 56-bit keys (broken). RC4 has multiple cryptographic flaws. AES with appropriate key length (128/192/256) and AEAD mode is the current standard.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Types of Ciphers — ECB, CBC, OFB & More

stem: Which CPU feature explicitly marks memory pages as non-executable to prevent execution of injected shellcode?
explanation: DEP (Data Execution Prevention) using the hardware NX bit marks data pages non-executable. ASLR randomises addresses; stack canaries detect overflow; ROP-guard targets return-oriented programming. DEP+ASLR is the baseline OS hardening combo against memory-corruption exploits.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Secure boot ensures that:
choices: The OS boots from any media
Each stage of the boot chain verifies a signature on the next stage before executing
explanation: Secure boot establishes a chain of trust: UEFI verifies bootloader, bootloader verifies kernel, etc. Any unsigned or modified component halts the chain. Encryption of the bootloader is unrelated. The other choices misdescribe the mechanism.

web_sources.title: ThreatOnTheWire: Securing the Hardware Platform — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which key length is the MINIMUM AES key size considered acceptable for protecting CLASSIFIED data per CNSA Suite (Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite)?
explanation: CNSA 2.0 requires AES-256 for symmetric encryption of TOP SECRET data. AES-128 is acceptable for SECRET-and-below in CNSA 1.0 but the 2024 CNSA 2.0 update raises requirements. AES-512 does not exist as a standard. CNSA also addresses post-quantum migration.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5: Recommendation for Key Management

stem: Which fire-suppression agent is INAPPROPRIATE for an occupied datacenter due to suffocation risk?
explanation: CO₂ at firefighting concentrations is lethal — it MUST not be used in occupied spaces. FM-200, Novec 1230, and Inergen are designed to be safe at design concentrations. Modern datacenters favor clean agents over CO₂ for this reason.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which model uses subjects, objects, and a security label lattice with read/write rules but ALLOWS for limited 'trusted subjects' to violate the *-property as needed for system administration?
explanation: Bell-LaPadula explicitly recognises 'trusted subjects' that can violate strict rules under controlled conditions (e.g., a system admin downgrading data after declassification). Biba does not have an analogous concept. Brewer-Nash is dynamic. Information-flow models are the broader theoretical class.

web_sources.title: SIIT: CISSP Security Models in Exams

stem: Which model formally describes how rights can be passed between subjects via 'take' and 'grant' operations?
explanation: Take-Grant analyses authorised propagation of rights using directed graphs and four primitives. Graham-Denning provides eight rules for creating/deleting subjects, objects, and rights. Bell-LaPadula and Biba focus on access decisions, not propagation analysis.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which control type does a 'guard' (in the cross-domain solution sense) primarily implement?
choices: Filtering of data traversing security domains based on inspection and policy
explanation: A guard inspects content and metadata moving between security domains and either passes, sanitises, or blocks per policy (e.g., MILS systems, HSTS guards). Encryption is unrelated; NAT is layer-3 translation; auditing is observation, not enforcement.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: An organisation needs to encrypt a 1 GB file for a colleague. Which approach is BEST?
choices: Encrypt the file directly with the colleague's RSA-2048 public key
Generate a random AES-256 session key, encrypt the file with AES, then encrypt only the session key with the colleague's RSA public key (hybrid encryption)
Use a shared password with PBKDF2
explanation: Hybrid encryption (symmetric for bulk + asymmetric for the key) is the pragmatic standard — RSA cannot encrypt large data efficiently. PBKDF2 + shared password requires out-of-band key sharing. Signing provides integrity, not confidentiality. TLS, S/MIME, PGP all use hybrid encryption.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which is the BEST mitigation for length-extension attacks on hash-based MACs?
choices: Use HMAC instead of plain hash
Concatenate the secret key after the message
explanation: HMAC's nested structure prevents length-extension attacks that affect Merkle-Damgård hashes (SHA-1, SHA-256). Plain `H(secret || message)` is vulnerable. Concatenating the key at the end (`H(message || secret)`) is also weaker than HMAC. ECB is unrelated.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: Which capability ensures a process cannot interfere with another's memory or device access?
choices: Process isolation enforced by the operating system / hypervisor
explanation: Process/memory isolation enforced by OS kernel and CPU MMU separation prevents cross-process interference. Antivirus catches known bad code. Logging is observation. RAID is storage redundancy. Isolation is the mechanism that prevents the interference, not the detective controls.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which is the PRIMARY purpose of a security kernel?
choices: To run with maximum privileges only
To implement the reference monitor concept — mediating all access between subjects and objects
explanation: The security kernel implements the reference monitor — mediating all access decisions enforceable by the TCB. Privilege is a property; firewalls and compression are unrelated. The security kernel is the realisation of the reference-monitor concept in code.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: In a SaaS deployment, which security responsibility is MOST clearly retained by the customer?
choices: Identity and access management for the customer's users; data classification; data ingest decisions
Maintaining the data center physical security
explanation: Even in SaaS, customers retain responsibility for who has access (IAM), what data goes in, and how it is classified. Provider handles infrastructure, platform, and most of the application. Knowing the SaaS responsibility line is high-yield for the exam.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 3 — Comprehensive Security Architecture Guide

stem: Which is the BEST description of 'salt' in password hashing?
choices: A pepper added to the database
Random per-user data concatenated with the password before hashing to defeat precomputed rainbow tables
explanation: Salt is unique per-credential random data, stored in the clear with the hash, that prevents precomputed rainbow-table reuse and ensures identical passwords have different hashes. 'Pepper' is a distinct per-system secret. The other choices misdescribe salt.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Cryptography MindMap — CISSP Domain 3

stem: At which OSI layer do MAC addresses operate?
explanation: MAC addresses are layer-2 (Data Link) identifiers used by Ethernet, Wi-Fi, etc. IP addresses are layer-3. Physical layer concerns voltages and signaling. Transport handles ports and connection state. Mnemonic: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' for OSI layers 1-7.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: At which OSI layer does TLS operate?
choices: Layer 7 (Application) — though commonly described as 'between L4 and L7'
explanation: TLS sits above TCP (L4) and below applications (L7); CISSP commonly classifies it at the session/presentation layers (L5/L6) or treats it as L7. Choice D is the best of the four. The exam tends to accept 'session/presentation' or 'application-level encryption' depending on framing.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which TLS version is the FIRST to mandate forward secrecy and remove RSA key transport?
explanation: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) removed RSA key transport and weak ciphers, mandating (EC)DHE for forward secrecy and AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). Earlier versions allowed static-RSA cipher suites. TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated; 1.2 is still common but lacks the 1.3 simplifications.

web_sources.title: RFC 8446: TLS 1.3

stem: Which IPsec component provides confidentiality and integrity for the IP payload?
explanation: ESP encrypts the payload (and optionally authenticates it). AH provides integrity-only over the immutable IP header and payload but no confidentiality. IKE negotiates the SAs. NAT-T encapsulates ESP in UDP/4500 to traverse NAT. AH BREAKS through NAT because NAT mutates header fields AH protects.

web_sources.title: RFC 4301: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol (IPsec)
RFC 4303: IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)

stem: Which IPsec mode encrypts ONLY the payload, leaving the original IP header in the clear?
explanation: Transport mode (host-to-host) encrypts only the payload — original IP header is visible. Tunnel mode (gateway-to-gateway) encapsulates the entire original IP packet inside a new IP header — used for site-to-site VPNs. ESP and AH are protocols, not modes.

web_sources.title: RFC 4301: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol (IPsec)

stem: Which DNS extension provides cryptographic origin authentication and integrity for DNS responses?
explanation: DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records, proving authenticity and integrity. DoH/DoT/DoQ provide privacy/transport encryption — they prevent eavesdropping but do not authenticate the data. Both are useful and address different problems; DNSSEC is the data-authentication answer.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which wireless security mechanism uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) to replace WPA2's pre-shared key handshake?
explanation: WPA3-Personal uses SAE (a Dragonfly-derived PAKE) instead of WPA2's PSK 4-way handshake, which was vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks if the handshake was captured. WEP and WPA are obsolete. WPA2-PSK uses a less secure 4-way handshake.

web_sources.title: IronWiFi: Best EAP Methods for Wi-Fi — EAP-TLS vs PEAP vs EAP-TTLS
Cloudi-Fi: WPA2/3-Enterprise — Secure Wi-Fi with 802.1X authentication

stem: Which EAP method is considered the gold standard for enterprise wireless authentication, providing mutual certificate-based authentication?
explanation: EAP-TLS uses certificates on both client and server for mutual authentication — strongest but operationally heavier (requires PKI). PEAP and EAP-TTLS use server-side certificates with inner authentication. EAP-MD5 is weak and obsolete. WPA3-Enterprise prefers EAP-TLS.

web_sources.title: SmallStep: Certificate Based Wi-Fi Authentication with RADIUS and EAP-TLS

stem: Which 802.11 attack pattern relies on broadcasting deauthentication frames to disconnect victims and force them to reconnect to a rogue AP?
explanation: Evil twin (rogue AP) attacks often use deauth frames to kick clients off legitimate APs and lure them to attacker-controlled APs with the same SSID. WPA3 includes Protected Management Frames (PMF/802.11w) to defeat deauth attacks. The other choices target other layers/protocols.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which type of firewall maintains a state table of connections and makes decisions based on connection state in addition to packet headers?
explanation: Stateful inspection tracks TCP connection state, allowing return traffic for established sessions automatically — the modern baseline. Packet-filter firewalls examine each packet in isolation. Application firewalls (proxies) inspect L7 content. Bastion hosts are hardened entry points, not a firewall type.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: A Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) DIFFERS from a stateful firewall PRIMARILY by:
choices: Adding application identification, IPS capability, and often integrated threat intelligence
explanation: NGFWs add application awareness (decoding L7 protocols), integrated IPS, and threat-intel-driven blocking — beyond simple stateful tracking. They still operate across multiple layers. They don't eliminate VPNs. Behavioral and anomaly-based detection are increasingly common alongside signatures.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which device type SPECIFICALLY inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic for application-layer attacks like SQL injection and XSS?
explanation: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) operates at L7 specifically for HTTP/HTTPS, applying rules from sources like the OWASP Core Rule Set. Generic IDS/IPS may have web rules but are not specialized. NAT gateways are network-layer translation, not security devices in this sense.

web_sources.title: OWASP Top Ten Project
DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which is the BEST description of zero trust networking?
choices: Place all internal users in a trusted zone behind the perimeter
Assume the network is hostile and require continuous authentication, authorisation, and least-privilege access on a per-resource basis
Trust users for 24 hours after authentication
explanation: Zero trust treats every request as untrusted and requires verification of identity, device posture, context, and authorisation per resource. The classic perimeter-trust model (choice A) is what zero trust replaces. Continuous validation is core; long-lived sessions violate the model.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture
Cisco Duo: Zero Trust Segmentation Guide for Security Leaders

stem: Which is the PRIMARY benefit of microsegmentation?
choices: Limiting east-west lateral movement after an initial compromise
explanation: Microsegmentation enforces fine-grained workload-to-workload policy, choking lateral movement after a breach. Throughput and physical hardware are not improved. VLANs may still be used as substrates. Microsegmentation is a key enabler of zero-trust architectures.

web_sources.title: IPwithEase: Microsegmentation vs Zero Trust
Cisco Duo: Zero Trust Segmentation Guide for Security Leaders

stem: What is a CORE characteristic of Software-Defined Networking (SDN)?
choices: Decoupling the control plane from the data plane
explanation: SDN separates the control plane (decision-making) from the data plane (forwarding) and centralises control logic, enabling programmatic, policy-driven networks. The other choices are unrelated or false.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) for Scalable Security

stem: Which network virtualisation technology extends Layer-2 segments over a Layer-3 underlay using UDP encapsulation?
explanation: VXLAN (RFC 7348) encapsulates L2 frames in UDP packets (default port 4789) to extend L2 across L3 underlays — common in cloud and data centers. MPLS uses label switching. GRE is a generic tunnel protocol. PPP is point-to-point. VXLAN does NOT provide encryption by default.

explanation: ARP spoofing sends forged ARP replies so victims send traffic to the attacker. DNS poisoning corrupts name resolution. MAC flooding overflows switch CAM tables to force hub-like behaviour. Smurf attacks ICMP-amplify against broadcast addresses. Mitigations include DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection).

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which attack pattern uses ICMP echo requests with a spoofed source address to a broadcast network, causing all hosts to respond and overwhelm the spoofed victim?
explanation: Smurf attacks amplify by ICMP broadcast. Fraggle is the UDP variant. Teardrop sends overlapping IP fragments. Ping of Death sends an oversized ICMP packet. Modern routers drop directed broadcasts (RFC 2644), making Smurf historic.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which mitigation for SYN-flood DoS is BUILT INTO the TCP stack?
explanation: SYN cookies (Bernstein) encode connection state into the initial sequence number rather than holding half-open connections, allowing the server to verify a returning ACK without state. The other choices target unrelated attacks.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a DMZ (demilitarised zone) in network architecture?
choices: Provide an isolated network segment for systems that must be reachable from the internet, separating them from the internal network
explanation: A DMZ segregates internet-facing services so a compromise does not directly expose the internal network. The other choices are unrelated to DMZ purpose. Modern equivalents include screened subnets, public subnets in cloud, or service-mesh ingress zones.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which VPN type is BEST for a remote user accessing internal corporate resources via a web browser without installing a client?
explanation: SSL/TLS VPNs (often called clientless VPNs) use the browser's TLS stack to access web-based internal apps — no client install needed. IPsec site-to-site connects networks, not individuals. PPTP is obsolete. L2TP without IPsec lacks confidentiality.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which is the PRIMARY purpose of NAC (Network Access Control)?
choices: Verify endpoint identity and posture before allowing network access; remediate non-compliant devices
explanation: NAC enforces identity + posture (patches, AV, configuration) before granting access — and may quarantine non-compliant devices. It often uses 802.1X as the access-control mechanism rather than replacing it. DHCP is unrelated to access control.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which is the PRIMARY confidentiality risk in unencrypted VoIP?
choices: Traffic is captured by anyone on the path and conversation can be reconstructed
explanation: Unencrypted SIP/RTP can be captured and conversations reconstructed (Wireshark even has built-in reconstruction). SIPS (TLS-protected SIP) and SRTP (encrypted RTP) mitigate this. The other choices are operational, not security, concerns.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which IDS detection method is MOST EFFECTIVE at finding NEW (zero-day) attacks?
explanation: Anomaly-based detection learns normal baselines and flags deviations — including novel attacks. Signature-based misses zero-days by definition. Packet inspection is a method, not a detection class. Port mirroring is a delivery mechanism.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
choices: An IDS is hardware; an IPS is software
An IPS actively blocks detected threats; an IDS only alerts
An IDS is faster; an IPS is slower
explanation: IDS = detection + alert (passive). IPS = detection + active blocking (inline, can drop traffic). The form-factor difference is unrelated. Inline operation makes IPS performance-critical; misconfigurations can cause outages.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which technology validates that an inbound email's sending IP is authorised by the sender domain's DNS records?
explanation: SPF lists authorised sending IPs in DNS TXT records; receivers check against the envelope sender. DKIM adds cryptographic signatures over headers/body. DMARC ties SPF + DKIM to policy + reporting. S/MIME signs/encrypts message content end-to-end. The trio (SPF + DKIM + DMARC) is the modern email-anti-spoofing baseline.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which protocol provides end-to-end encryption AND digital signatures for email message content?
explanation: S/MIME (and PGP) provide content-level encryption and signatures end-to-end. SPF/DKIM/DMARC address envelope-level anti-spoofing and policy. The exam differentiates content security from infrastructure security.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: What is the PRIMARY enterprise concern with DNS over HTTPS (DoH) deployed by end-user browsers?
choices: Bypasses traditional enterprise DNS-based monitoring and policy enforcement
explanation: DoH on port 443 hides DNS queries from network-layer enterprise controls (DNS firewall, RPZ, sinkholing). DoT (port 853) is more visible but still encrypts. Many enterprises prefer DoT or proxy-controlled DoH endpoints. Latency/cost are minor.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which is the PRIMARY security benefit of a CDN with DDoS scrubbing?
choices: Absorbing volumetric attacks across distributed POPs and serving cached content during incidents
Eliminating the need for application security
explanation: CDNs deliver capacity and geographic distribution that absorb volumetric DDoS, and they continue serving cached content while origin recovers. They do not eliminate the need for app-layer security (WAF, secure coding). The other choices are unrelated benefits or false.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: What is the PRIMARY security benefit (incidental) of NAT/PAT?
choices: Internal addresses are not directly routable from the internet, providing some obscurity
explanation: NAT/PAT was designed for IPv4 address conservation; the security side effect is internal hosts are not directly addressable from outside (security through translation). It is NOT a real security control — it is an obscurity benefit. Layer-7 attacks still pass through NAT.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: TLS 1.3's 0-RTT mode improves performance by allowing data in the first flight, but introduces what risk?
choices: Replay of the 0-RTT data, since 0-RTT does not have full forward-secrecy / replay protection on its own
explanation: TLS 1.3 0-RTT (early data) lacks the full anti-replay protections of the standard handshake — servers should restrict 0-RTT to idempotent operations and use server-side anti-replay where critical. Certificate validation is unaffected. CPU may be reduced, not increased.

web_sources.title: RFC 8446: TLS 1.3

stem: Which 802.11 frame type allows attackers to disconnect clients without breaking encryption when Protected Management Frames (PMF) are NOT enabled?
explanation: Deauth frames are management-class, traditionally unprotected — easily forged to disconnect victims. 802.11w / Protected Management Frames protects management frames against forgery. Other frame types are not the canonical disconnection vector.

web_sources.title: Cloudi-Fi: WPA2/3-Enterprise — Secure Wi-Fi with 802.1X authentication

stem: What is the PRIMARY security concern when adopting SD-WAN over public internet links?
choices: Tunnels are typically point-to-point, traffic inside encrypted tunnels lacks per-flow inspection without a SASE/security overlay
explanation: SD-WAN tunnels (often IPsec or VXLAN) provide point-to-point confidentiality but lack inline security inspection without a paired security stack (SASE). The other choices are operational concerns or false.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) for Scalable Security

stem: Which is the BEST mitigation for legacy ICS/SCADA devices that cannot be patched without operational disruption?
choices: Network segmentation, monitoring, and protocol-aware firewalls between IT and OT
explanation: OT environments require segmentation (Purdue model), passive monitoring (e.g., NIDS for ICS protocols), and OT-aware firewalls. Internet exposure is dangerous; disabling logging hides incidents; immediate cloud migration is rarely feasible due to operational constraints.

stem: Which network design pattern BEST supports protecting IoT devices that cannot run modern security agents?

Dedicated IoT VLAN/segment with restrictive ACLs and outbound-only access to known endpoints
Encrypt only IoT data at rest
explanation: Segmenting IoT into dedicated VLANs with restrictive policy limits blast radius. Flat networks let IoT compromises pivot to high-value systems. Disabling IoT is impractical. At-rest encryption alone misses network exposure.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

choices: 802.1X with NAC posture assessment and dynamic VLAN assignment
explanation: 802.1X authentication paired with NAC posture (patch level, AV running, certificate-based device identity) and dynamic VLAN assignment is the modern enterprise pattern. MAC filtering is trivially spoofable. Static IP is administrative, not security control.

explanation: Two-firewall (front and back) screened subnets create layered policies; using different vendors limits single-bug or single-misconfiguration exposure. Cost and speed are not the rationale. IDS still complements firewalls.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which control prevents data exfiltration via DNS tunneling MOST effectively?

Allow direct DNS to any resolver
explanation: Forcing DNS through enterprise resolvers and applying analytics (large payloads, high entropy, suspicious TXT volumes) detects/blocks DNS tunneling. Blocking all DNS breaks the network. Direct DNS to any resolver is permissive. DoH alone hides DNS without analytics.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which protocol provides TIME synchronisation that is OFTEN under-prioritised but CRITICAL for log correlation and Kerberos?
explanation: NTP keeps clocks in sync; large skew breaks Kerberos (ticket validity windows) and confuses correlation across devices. The exam frequently asks why NTP matters for security. The other protocols serve different purposes.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which is the PRIMARY security benefit of mTLS (mutual TLS) between microservices?
choices: Both client and server authenticate cryptographically, providing strong workload identity
Eliminates the need for service mesh
explanation: mTLS provides cryptographic mutual authentication between services using certificates — strong workload identity. Authorisation is still required (mTLS proves who, policy decides what). Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) often automate mTLS. Performance is not the primary benefit.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security
NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture

stem: Which DDoS attack TYPE targets the application layer with low-volume but expensive requests (e.g., Slowloris)?
explanation: L7 attacks (Slowloris, HTTP flood, RUDY) consume server resources rather than bandwidth — low-volume but devastating to specific apps. Volumetric saturates link capacity. Protocol attacks abuse stack weaknesses (SYN flood). Reflective amplification (DNS, NTP, memcached) leverages third-party servers.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which DMARC policy value tells receivers to REJECT messages that fail SPF and DKIM alignment?
explanation: DMARC has three policies: none (monitor only), quarantine (treat as suspicious), reject (drop). 'accept' is not a DMARC value. Organisations typically progress none → quarantine → reject as confidence in alignment grows.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which is the BEST way to deliver web application access to remote users WITHOUT placing them on the corporate network?
choices: Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) brokered access, identity- and context-aware, with no broad network reachability
explanation: ZTNA grants per-application access based on identity and context, never exposing broad network ranges (a major shift from VPN). Open RDP is dangerous. Site-to-site VPNs to homes are operationally infeasible. MAC ACLs cannot follow remote users.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture
Cisco Duo: Zero Trust Segmentation Guide for Security Leaders

choices: SAE handshake (Dragonfly), each session derives a unique key
explanation: SAE establishes a unique session key per handshake — capturing one session does not compromise others, and offline PSK guessing against captured handshakes is no longer feasible. The other choices are unrelated or dangerous (WEP fallback would be a regression).

web_sources.title: IronWiFi: Best EAP Methods for Wi-Fi — EAP-TLS vs PEAP vs EAP-TTLS

explanation: Without strict server-cert validation, attackers can stand up rogue RADIUS servers and harvest inner credentials (MSCHAPv2). Enforcing server-cert validation (and migrating to EAP-TLS where feasible) closes this gap. The other choices are insecure.

IronWiFi: Best EAP Methods for Wi-Fi — EAP-TLS vs PEAP vs EAP-TTLS

choices: Allow-all by default; block specific bad
Deny-all by default; allow specific business need
explanation: Default-deny is the secure baseline; rules grant only specific business need. Default-allow lists are unmanageable and miss novel attacks. Outbound rules also matter for egress control. Choice C and D are wrong (one is permissive, one breaks operations).

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which attack relies on intercepting and altering messages in transit between two parties who believe they are communicating directly?
explanation: MITM intercepts and may modify messages — TLS with strict cert validation defeats it; SSH host-key verification mitigates it. Replay reuses captured messages. Brute force tries credentials. Smurf is amplification.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which SDN component is the SINGLE point of failure that MUST be hardened and made highly available?
explanation: The SDN controller centralises decisions — its compromise or outage affects the whole network. Hardening (RBAC, mTLS) and HA (clustering) are essential. Data plane switches are distributed; APIs are interfaces, not core failure points.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) for Scalable Security

stem: Which protocol is BEST for secure interactive remote command-line access?
explanation: SSH provides encrypted authentication and session encryption. Telnet, FTP, and TFTP transmit credentials/data in cleartext (deprecated in any modern environment). SSH-keys with strong passphrases or hardware tokens are the standard.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which is the BEST control to prevent rogue access points on the corporate network?
choices: Trust users not to install them
Wireless intrusion detection (WIDS) combined with 802.1X port security on wired ports
explanation: WIDS detects unauthorised radios; 802.1X port security prevents rogue APs from being plugged in successfully. Trust alone fails; full Wi-Fi disablement is impractical; band selection does not address rogue devices.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which is the PRIMARY purpose of a DNS Firewall (Response Policy Zone, RPZ)?
choices: Block resolution of malicious domains based on threat intelligence feeds
explanation: DNS RPZ allows applying threat-intel-based policy at the resolver level (block/redirect/sinkhole). Speed, compression, and zone-transfer security (TSIG) are unrelated. RPZ is a high-value defensive layer for catching command-and-control communications.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 4 — Guide to Communication and Network Security

stem: Which AAA element answers the question 'who are you?'
explanation: Authentication answers 'are you who you claim to be?' Identification (claiming identity) precedes authentication. Authorisation answers 'what may you do?'. Accounting (auditing) records what was done. CISSP often uses I-A-A-A (identification, authentication, authorisation, accounting).

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: A hardware security key (e.g., FIDO2 token) represents which authentication factor?
explanation: Hardware tokens are 'something you have'. 'Know' covers passwords/PINs. 'Are' covers biometrics. 'Somewhere' (location) is sometimes included as a fourth factor. NIST 800-63B treats FIDO2/WebAuthn as a multi-factor cryptographic authenticator and the only widely deployed one resistant to verifier impersonation at AAL3.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-63-3: Digital Identity Guidelines
CISSPrep: Access Control Systems, MFA & Biometrics

stem: Which is NOT considered TRUE multi-factor authentication?
explanation: Two pieces of 'something you know' (password + security question) are SAME-FACTOR — both knowledge. Real MFA combines distinct factor categories (know/have/are). Smart card + PIN is the canonical have+know example.

web_sources.title: Medium / The Effective CISSP: Multi-Factor Authentication (Wentz Wu)

stem: Which IAM lifecycle issue is BEST mitigated by automated provisioning and deprovisioning tied to HR systems?
explanation: When HR triggers provisioning/deprovisioning, role changes and terminations cascade automatically — preventing privilege creep (accumulating rights as roles change) and orphaned accounts (active accounts of departed users). Password and brute-force/phishing are addressed by other controls.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: How often should privileged access for high-risk systems be reviewed at MINIMUM?
choices: Quarterly or more frequently with continuous monitoring
explanation: Privileged access reviews on critical systems should be at least quarterly, ideally continuous (e.g., automated drift detection). Annual is the floor for low-risk systems. Manager-mindset answers favor frequent reviews where stakes are high.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which access control model assigns rights based on the job FUNCTION the user holds?
explanation: RBAC (Role-Based) ties permissions to roles; users get permissions by being members of roles. DAC lets the data owner grant rights ad-hoc. MAC uses labels enforced by the system. ABAC uses attributes (user, resource, environment) for fine-grained policy. Production systems often layer RBAC + ABAC.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which access control model is BEST for a system that must enforce CLASSIFICATION-based access (e.g., government Top Secret data)?
explanation: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) uses subject clearances and object labels enforced by the system — appropriate for classified environments. DAC lets owners grant access (less rigorous). RBAC and rule-based don't directly model the classification lattice required by government policy.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which access control model is the MOST flexible, allowing decisions based on user, resource, action, and environmental attributes simultaneously?
explanation: ABAC (Attribute-Based) supports complex policies like 'user must be in HR, resource must be HR data, time must be business hours, device must be managed' — far more expressive than RBAC alone. NIST SP 800-162 is the ABAC reference.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: In Kerberos, which component issues TGS (Service) tickets after presentation of a TGT?
explanation: Kerberos flow: AS authenticates the user and issues a TGT. The client presents the TGT to the TGS to receive service tickets. The service then validates the service ticket. Kerberos requires synchronised clocks (NTP) — typical skew tolerance is ~5 minutes.

web_sources.title: RFC 4120: The Kerberos Network Authentication Service (V5)

stem: Which is a known weakness of Kerberos that admins MUST mitigate?
choices: Reliance on a single Key Distribution Center (KDC) — a SPOF and high-value target
explanation: The KDC is a single point of failure and a high-value attack target. HA replication, hardening, and monitoring are essential. Kerberos provides confidentiality of credentials. Service tickets are core to the protocol. Password policy is enforced by realm policy.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which protocol uses XML-based assertions exchanged between an Identity Provider and a Service Provider for federated authentication?
explanation: SAML 2.0 uses XML assertions (authentication, attribute, authorization) typically over HTTP-Redirect/POST bindings. OAuth 2.0 is for delegated authorisation, OIDC adds an authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 (using JWTs). RADIUS is for AAA against network resources, not browser-based federation.
