Fortinet: What is SAML vs OAuth?

stem: Which is the BEST description of OAuth 2.0?
choices: An authorisation framework that allows third-party apps to obtain limited access to a resource on behalf of the user
explanation: OAuth 2.0 is delegated AUTHORISATION — it issues access tokens granting scoped resource access. It is NOT an authentication protocol on its own (a common exam trap). OpenID Connect adds an ID token (JWT) on top of OAuth 2.0 for authentication.

web_sources.title: RFC 6749: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
Fortinet: What is SAML vs OAuth?

stem: Which is the BEST description of OpenID Connect (OIDC)?
choices: An authentication layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds an ID token (JWT) for user authentication
explanation: OIDC adds an authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 — the ID token (a JWT) carries identity claims. It is widely used for modern web/mobile authentication. OIDC complements OAuth, doesn't replace it. JWTs are JSON not XML.

web_sources.title: OpenID Connect: Core Specifications
SecurityJourney: OpenID Connect vs OAuth 2.0 vs SAML 2.0

stem: Which protocol encrypts ONLY the password field and uses UDP, traditionally used for network device AAA?
explanation: RADIUS (RFC 2865) uses UDP and only encrypts the password attribute. TACACS+ encrypts the entire payload over TCP. Diameter is the next-gen protocol with stronger transport security. Kerberos is unrelated to network AAA. CISSP frequently tests these distinctions.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which protocol provides full payload encryption AND separation of authentication, authorisation, and accounting?
explanation: TACACS+ (Cisco/IETF) encrypts the entire packet body over TCP and separates A/A/A — beneficial for granular command authorisation on network devices. RADIUS combines AuthN+AuthZ and only encrypts password. Kerberos and LDAP serve different purposes.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Per modern NIST SP 800-63B guidance, which password practice is NOT recommended?
choices: Allow long passphrases up to 64 characters
Periodic forced password expiration without cause
Avoid composition rules (mixed case, special chars)
explanation: NIST 800-63B explicitly removed periodic forced expiration as a default — research showed it pushes users toward predictable patterns. Forced rotation is justified ONLY on suspicion of compromise. Long passphrases, breached-password checks, and dropping composition rules are recommended.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-63-3: Digital Identity Guidelines

stem: Which authentication factor type is generally considered LEAST secure on its own?
explanation: SMS OTP is vulnerable to SIM swap and SS7 attacks; NIST 800-63B classifies SMS as RESTRICTED (not banned, but discouraged). FIDO2 is the strongest. Number-matching push reduces fatigue attacks. TPM-backed biometrics are also strong.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-63-3: Digital Identity Guidelines

stem: Which is the BEST mitigation for the risk of long-standing privileged accounts?
choices: Just-In-Time (JIT) elevation — grant privileges only when needed and time-limit them
Allow shared admin accounts for convenience
explanation: JIT access removes standing privilege — admins request elevation, get it for a bounded window, and lose it after. PAM tools enforce this. Stronger passwords help but standing privilege remains exposed. Disabling MFA and shared accounts are anti-patterns.

web_sources.title: ThorTeaches: Just-in-Time (JIT) access glossary
CyberArk: What is Just-In-Time Access?

stem: Which is the PRIMARY purpose of a Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution?
choices: Vault privileged credentials, broker sessions, record activity, and rotate secrets automatically
explanation: PAM provides credential vaulting, session brokering with recording, and automatic rotation — the core controls for privileged accounts. End-user passwords are managed by IDPs / authenticators. Choices C and D misunderstand PAM scope.

web_sources.title: CyberArk: What is Just-In-Time Access?
DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which is a PRIMARY risk of single sign-on (SSO)?
choices: Compromise of the SSO credentials grants attackers access to all federated applications
explanation: SSO concentrates risk: one credential compromise pivots to many resources. Mitigations include MFA, conditional access, anomaly detection, short session lifetimes, and step-up authentication for sensitive actions. Friction reduction is a benefit, not a risk.

web_sources.title: ExamCollection: Comprehensive Guide to SSO for CISSP

stem: In a SAML federation, which entity is the IdP (Identity Provider)?
choices: The application the user wants to access
The system that authenticates the user and issues SAML assertions
explanation: The IdP authenticates the user (e.g., Okta, Azure AD). The application is the Service Provider (SP) which trusts the IdP's assertions. The browser carries assertions in HTTP-POST/Redirect bindings. The CA may issue signing certs but is not the IdP.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Federated Identity Management — Extensive CISSP Guide
CISSPrep: Federation and SAML

stem: Which RBAC concept enforces that two specified roles cannot be assigned to the same user (e.g., a user cannot be both 'requester' and 'approver')?
explanation: SSoD prevents conflicting roles from being assigned to the same user at provisioning time. DSoD permits assignment but blocks simultaneous activation in one session (e.g., a user can have both roles but cannot activate them together). Hierarchy and delegation are different concepts.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which is the BEST mitigation for a SAML attack where attackers manipulate signed assertions due to XML signature wrapping flaws?
choices: Validate the signed element specifically AND verify the signature covers the asserting identity claims
explanation: XSW (XML Signature Wrapping) attacks exploit parsers that validate one element while consuming another. Mitigation: validate signed element identity explicitly; use modern libraries; restrict to expected elements. Disabling signatures or trusting blindly defeats security entirely.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Federated Identity Management — Extensive CISSP Guide

stem: Which session management practice MOST reduces session-fixation risk?
choices: Generate a NEW session ID on authentication and on privilege change
Pin sessions to source IP only
explanation: Regenerating session IDs on auth/privilege escalation defeats session fixation (where the attacker plants a known session ID and convinces the victim to authenticate into it). IP pinning is brittle (mobile users); never-expiring sessions are dangerous; reuse is the vulnerability itself.

web_sources.title: OWASP Top Ten Project

stem: What is the CROSSOVER ERROR RATE (CER or EER) of a biometric system?
choices: The point where false acceptance and false rejection rates are equal — lower is better
The maximum FAR allowed by policy
The number of biometric templates stored
explanation: CER/EER is the equal-error point — the lower it is, the more accurate the biometric. FAR (false acceptance) and FRR (false rejection) trade off; the CER is the operating point where they cross. The other choices are unrelated.

web_sources.title: CISSPrep: Access Control Systems, MFA & Biometrics

stem: Which biometric error type is MOST critical to MINIMISE in a high-security environment?
explanation: FAR (admitting an unauthorised user) is the security failure mode — must be minimised in high-security settings, even at the cost of higher FRR (legitimate users rejected). The exam tests this trade-off; you can re-attempt as a legitimate user, but a false acceptance is a breach.

web_sources.title: CISSPrep: Access Control Systems, MFA & Biometrics

stem: Which is the BEST example of an attribute-based access control rule?
choices: Allow access only if user.dept = resource.dept AND time between 0800-1800 AND device is managed
Allow all internal users by default
Allow access if user has a password
explanation: ABAC combines multiple attributes — user, resource, environment — into the policy decision. Choice A is RBAC. Choice C is open/permissive. Choice D is bare authentication, not authorisation. ABAC is what XACML, AWS IAM policies, and Azure AD conditional access implement.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which attack pattern targets Kerberos by requesting service tickets for high-privilege accounts and offline cracking the encrypted portion?
explanation: Kerberoasting requests TGS tickets for service accounts (which encrypt with the service's NTLM hash) and offline-cracks the ciphertext to recover the service password. Mitigations: long random service account passwords, gMSAs (group Managed Service Accounts), rotation. Pass-the-Hash, Golden Ticket, and DCSync are different AD attacks.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which Kerberos attack uses the KRBTGT account hash to forge arbitrary TGTs that grant impersonation of any user?
explanation: Golden Ticket attacks use the KRBTGT password hash (often retrieved via DCSync) to mint arbitrary TGTs — full domain compromise. Silver Tickets forge service tickets for individual services. Pass-the-Hash uses NTLM hashes. KRBTGT must be rotated TWICE consecutively to invalidate forged tickets.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which protocol is COMMONLY used to query a directory server (e.g., Active Directory) for user/group attributes?
explanation: LDAP (and its secure variant LDAPS over TLS) is the standard directory access protocol. Active Directory uses LDAP on port 389/636. SMTP, FTP, and NTP are unrelated. Note: LDAP without TLS exposes credentials and queries in cleartext.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Per NIST SP 800-63B, which account lockout configuration is recommended?
choices: Lock after a small number of failed attempts with throttling, while supporting offline attack defenses (rate-limiting, breach-password blocking)
Never lock — let users retry forever
explanation: NIST 800-63B recommends rate-limiting and lockouts that are not so aggressive they enable trivial DoS — combined with breach-password blocking and other defenses. Choice A is overly punitive; C provides no defense; D enables DoS through targeted lockouts.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-63-3: Digital Identity Guidelines

stem: Which access control model lets the owner of an object grant access at their discretion?
explanation: DAC (Discretionary Access Control) gives the data owner full control of who gets access — typical of file systems via ACLs (e.g., Unix permissions, Windows NTFS). MAC removes that discretion in favor of system-enforced labels. RBAC and ABAC use other policy bases.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: What is a JWT (JSON Web Token)?
choices: A compact, URL-safe, signed (and optionally encrypted) JSON token used for transmitting claims between parties
explanation: JWT (RFC 7519) is the JSON-based token format used in OIDC and many OAuth 2.0 flows. Compact, URL-safe, signed (JWS) or encrypted (JWE). Issues: don't store secrets in JWT, validate algorithm, beware 'none' alg.

web_sources.title: OpenID Connect: Core Specifications

stem: Which OAuth 2.0 grant type is RECOMMENDED for native and single-page apps to mitigate authorization-code interception?
choices: Authorization Code with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange)
explanation: PKCE (RFC 7636) prevents code interception attacks against public clients (mobile apps, SPAs). The Implicit grant is deprecated. ROPC sends user passwords through the client (anti-pattern). Client Credentials is for service-to-service.

web_sources.title: RFC 6749: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework

stem: Per NIST SP 800-63, which of the following BEST corresponds to AAL3 (highest authenticator assurance)?
choices: Hardware-based cryptographic authenticator providing verifier-impersonation resistance (e.g., FIDO2)
explanation: AAL3 requires a hardware-based cryptographic authenticator with verifier-impersonation resistance — FIDO2/WebAuthn is the only widely deployed option that meets it. Choices A, B, D are AAL1 or AAL2 at best. Knowledge-based questions don't qualify.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-63-3: Digital Identity Guidelines

stem: What is rule-based access control?
choices: A list of users with permissions
Access decisions based on a set of system-wide rules (often IF-THEN), independent of identity
explanation: Rule-based access uses system-wide rules (e.g., a firewall ACL deny rule applies to all users). Distinct from RBAC, which is identity-and-role driven. The other choices describe different models.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which is the BEST description of a 'risk-based' or 'adaptive' authentication strategy?
choices: Vary authentication strength based on context (location, device, behaviour, risk score)
explanation: Adaptive auth steps up requirements (push challenge, MFA, biometric) when risk signals fire — anomalous IP, new device, unusual time, sensitive resource. Always-MFA is fine but not adaptive; skipping auth is dangerous; passwords-only is weak.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which protocol is BEST for AAA against network access devices (switches, firewalls) that need granular per-command authorisation?
explanation: TACACS+ supports per-command authorisation and full payload encryption — preferred for network device administrative access. RADIUS combines authn+authz and is more common for end-user network access. OAuth/SAML target user-facing applications.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which is the BEST single control to prevent former employees from retaining access to corporate systems?
choices: Automated deprovisioning triggered by HR termination event with same-day account disable
explanation: HR-triggered automated deprovisioning at the moment of termination closes the account-orphaning window definitively. Manual reviews leave gaps. Self-service deprovisioning is rare and unreliable. Password rotation alone leaves accounts active.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which is REQUIRED for Kerberos to function correctly in a network?
choices: Tightly synchronised time (typically within ~5 minutes via NTP)
explanation: Kerberos uses time-bound tickets — clock skew beyond ~5 minutes (configurable) breaks authentication. Hence the importance of NTP. The other choices are unrelated to Kerberos requirements.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which is the PRIMARY benefit of federation between two organisations?
choices: Users authenticate to their home organisation; the partner organisation trusts the assertion — no shared password store
Eliminates the need for any access control
explanation: Federation removes the need to provision separate accounts at each partner — users continue using their home credentials, with assertions exchanged between IdPs and SPs. Choice C and D are unrelated; choice A may be incidental but is not the primary benefit.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Federated Identity Management — Extensive CISSP Guide

stem: Which standard provides a schema and protocol for cross-domain identity management (provisioning)?
explanation: SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management, RFC 7644) standardises user provisioning between IdPs and SaaS providers. SAML/OIDC handle authentication; OAuth handles delegated authorisation. SCIM closes the provisioning lifecycle gap.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which is the BEST mitigation for MFA push-bombing / fatigue attacks?

explanation: Number-matching (user types a number shown on the login screen into the authenticator) defeats blind acceptance during fatigue attacks. Rate-limiting suppresses storming. Disabling MFA, permanent acceptance, and SMS-only are weakening choices.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which is the BEST approach to authorise an end user calling a microservice that itself calls multiple downstream services?
choices: Re-prompt the user at each downstream call
Forward the user's bearer token via OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange or constrained delegation
Use a single shared admin token
explanation: Token Exchange (RFC 8693) or service-to-service delegation maintains the user context downstream while limiting scope. Shared admin tokens lose context and over-privilege. Skipping internal authorisation violates zero-trust. Re-prompting is unworkable.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which is the PRIMARY benefit of centralized authentication vs. each application managing its own user store?
choices: Consistent policy enforcement, single source of truth, simpler deprovisioning, and federated SSO
explanation: Centralization (via IdP) means one policy, one source of truth, and one deprovisioning path — operationally and security-wise superior to per-app silos. Choice A is incidental; choice C is wrong (HA is critical); choice D is the opposite of intent.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which authentication mechanism uses a secret derived from a synchronised counter or time, NOT requiring server connectivity to verify?
explanation: TOTP (RFC 6238) and HOTP (RFC 4226) generate codes from a shared secret + time/counter — verifier checks locally. SMS requires telecom delivery. Push needs a back-channel. FIDO2 uses asymmetric crypto with the verifier. TOTP is widely deployed via Authenticator apps.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-63-3: Digital Identity Guidelines

stem: Which is the BEST description of the principle of least privilege?
choices: Users have the maximum needed for their entire career
Users have only the minimum permissions required for their CURRENT task or role
Users have administrative rights to be productive
explanation: Least privilege grants only what is needed RIGHT NOW for the role — combined with periodic review and JIT for elevation. Choices A, C, D contradict the principle. Saltzer & Schroeder formalised it as a foundational secure-design principle.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 5 — Identity & Access Management

stem: Which credential-recovery mechanism is GENERALLY the WEAKEST link in account security?
explanation: Knowledge-based recovery questions are widely guessable from social media or breach data — multiple high-profile compromises (e.g., 2008 Palin Yahoo breach) used them. NIST 800-63B discourages KBA. Backup tokens, recovery codes, and verified-email + MFA are stronger.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-63-3: Digital Identity Guidelines

stem: Which is the PRIMARY purpose of an entity's metadata in SAML federation?
choices: Publishing endpoints, certificates, and supported bindings so the partner can validate and route messages
explanation: SAML metadata (an XML document) declares endpoints, signing/encryption certificates, name ID formats, and bindings. Both IdP and SP exchange metadata to establish trust mechanically. The other choices are unrelated.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Federated Identity Management — Extensive CISSP Guide

stem: Which is the BEST way to manage shared privileged accounts that genuinely cannot be eliminated (e.g., legacy database accounts)?
choices: Vault credentials in PAM, broker each session with individual user attribution and recording, rotate after each use
Allow team members to share via chat
explanation: PAM with check-out, session brokering, attribution, recording, and post-use rotation provides accountability where the underlying account cannot be made user-specific. Documentation alone provides no control; sharing in chat is dangerous; disabling logging removes audit trail.

web_sources.title: CyberArk: What is Just-In-Time Access?

stem: Which is REQUIRED to validate a Kerberos service ticket?
choices: The service's secret (the shared key derived from the service account password)
explanation: The service uses its long-term secret (derived from its account password) to decrypt the service ticket and verify integrity. Long, random service-account passwords (or gMSAs) defend against Kerberoasting. The client password is not used at this step.

web_sources.title: RFC 4120: The Kerberos Network Authentication Service (V5)

stem: Which standard defines the SAML SP-Initiated Single Sign-On flow?
choices: OASIS SAML 2.0 Web Browser SSO Profile
explanation: OASIS standardised SAML 2.0 including the Web Browser SSO Profile (SP-initiated and IdP-initiated). RFC 6749 is OAuth 2.0; RFC 4120 is Kerberos; CTAP is the FIDO2 client-to-authenticator protocol.

web_sources.title: DestCert: Federated Identity Management — Extensive CISSP Guide

stem: Which testing technique inspects SOURCE CODE for security flaws WITHOUT running the application?
explanation: SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyses source/bytecode without execution — finding flaws like SQL injection patterns, hardcoded credentials, or insecure APIs. DAST runs against a running app. IAST instruments the running app. Fuzzing sends malformed inputs.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which testing technique exercises a RUNNING application from the outside, sending HTTP requests and observing responses?
explanation: DAST (Dynamic) is black-box-style runtime testing — sends crafted requests and identifies vulnerabilities by responses. SAST is static. Code review is manual SAST. Compliance scans verify configuration baselines, not application behaviour.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which technique INSTRUMENTS a running application to combine source-level visibility with runtime context?
explanation: IAST (Interactive) runs an agent inside the application, observing both code paths executed and runtime data — combining SAST's coverage with DAST's runtime accuracy. RASP (Runtime Application Self-Protection) actively blocks at runtime. SAST/DAST are static/dynamic.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Per NIST SP 800-115, which is NOT a phase of penetration testing?
explanation: NIST 800-115 defines four phases: Planning, Discovery, Attack, Reporting. Compliance certification is NOT a pen-test phase. PTES (Penetration Testing Execution Standard) defines seven, broader phases. The exam can ask either; specify the framework.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

stem: A 'gray box' penetration test BEST corresponds to which scenario?
choices: Attacker has partial information (e.g., user credentials and basic architecture)
explanation: Gray box simulates a partially informed attacker (e.g., compromised user, insider with limited info). Black box = no info; white box = full info; system owner is not an attacker model. Gray box maximises efficiency while testing realistic threat models.

web_sources.title: InfosecTrain: Black Box vs White Box vs Grey Box Penetration Testing
TraceSecurity: What is Black/White/Gray Box Testing?

stem: Which SOC report type evaluates security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy controls?
explanation: SOC 2 covers the AICPA Trust Services Criteria (security required, then availability/processing-integrity/confidentiality/privacy as elected). SOC 1 is financial reporting controls. SOC 3 is a public-summary version of SOC 2. SOC for cybersecurity is a separate program.

web_sources.title: SOCReports: ISAE 3402 Type 2 Reports — SOC 2 Audits
DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which difference distinguishes a SOC 2 Type II from Type I report?
choices: Type II evaluates operating effectiveness over a period (typically 6-12 months); Type I is design effectiveness at a point in time
explanation: Type I = design at a point in time. Type II = design + operating effectiveness over a period (e.g., 6 months). Type II provides more assurance for relying parties and is the typical deliverable to enterprise customers.

web_sources.title: Securance: ISAE 3402 / SOC 1 Type I vs Type II
BrandCompliance: SOC 2 or ISAE 3402?

stem: ISAE 3402 is the international equivalent of which SOC report?
explanation: ISAE 3402 mirrors SOC 1 (financial reporting controls). SOC 2 maps to ISAE 3000. CISSP candidates should know ISAE 3402 ≈ SOC 1 and ISAE 3000 ≈ SOC 2.

web_sources.title: SOCReports: ISAE 3402 Type 2 Reports — SOC 2 Audits
Zluri: ISAE 3402 vs SOC 2

stem: Which is the PRIMARY difference between vulnerability scanning and penetration testing?
choices: Pen tests attempt exploitation to demonstrate impact; vulnerability scans identify potential weaknesses without exploitation
explanation: Vulnerability scanning is breadth — produces a list of potential weaknesses (often noisy). Pen testing is depth — chains vulnerabilities to demonstrate real impact and verify exploitability. Both have a role in mature programs.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: What is the PRIMARY purpose of an authenticated vulnerability scan?
choices: Reveal vulnerabilities visible only to logged-in users (host-level patches, configurations)
explanation: Authenticated (credentialed) scans log into hosts and assess installed packages, missing patches, and config drift — invisible to unauthenticated network scans. Unauthenticated scans see only externally exposed surfaces. Both have a role.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the PRIMARY purpose of log review in a security program?
choices: Detect security events and provide forensic evidence after incidents
explanation: Log review supports detection (alerts on suspicious patterns) and post-incident forensics (reconstruction). It complements monitoring rather than replacing it. Software version tracking is inventory, not log review.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which property of logs is MOST important for forensic admissibility?
choices: Stored locally on the affected host
explanation: Logs must be tamper-evident (immutable storage, signing, hashing) and accurately timestamped. Local-only storage on a compromised host is the OPPOSITE of safe — log forwarding to a separate system is essential. Compression and formatting are operational.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Synthetic transactions are BEST described as:
choices: Scripted requests that simulate user actions to monitor availability and correctness
Fake user accounts created for testing
explanation: Synthetic transactions probe an application as a user would — confirming endpoints respond correctly and within SLA. Real-user monitoring (RUM) observes actual users. Backups and fake accounts are unrelated.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which type of code review is GENERALLY most effective at finding logic flaws and business-rule errors?
choices: Manual peer review by an experienced reviewer focused on logic and threat model
explanation: Manual peer review excels at logic and business-rule defects that automated tools miss (SAST sees patterns, not intent). The best programs combine SAST + manual review. Linting is style/syntax. Compilation catches structural errors only.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which document is THE MOST IMPORTANT to obtain BEFORE starting a penetration test?
choices: Authorisation letter and rules of engagement signed by an officer with authority to authorise the test
explanation: Without a signed authorisation (the 'get out of jail free' letter), pen testing is just unauthorised intrusion. Rules of engagement scope the test (targets, hours, escalation). The other choices are operational and not essential authorisation.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: How frequently should an organisation conduct external penetration tests at MINIMUM?
choices: Annually and after any major change
explanation: Annually + after major changes is the common industry baseline (PCI-DSS requires annually + after significant change). Many regulated industries require more frequent. Once-and-done or post-breach-only are inadequate; 5-year cycles are too long.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the BEST first action when a critical vulnerability is identified in a production system?
choices: Apply compensating controls and the vendor patch through change management as fast as risk dictates, prioritised by exploit availability and exposure
Wait for the next quarterly maintenance window
explanation: Manager-mindset: triage by risk (impact × exposure × exploit availability), apply compensating controls if patching takes time, push the patch through accelerated change management. Press releases are not first actions; waiting accumulates risk; disabling logging is anti-pattern.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which metric BEST functions as a KEY RISK indicator (KRI) rather than a KEY PERFORMANCE indicator (KPI)?
choices: Mean time to patch critical vulnerabilities
Number of unpatched critical vulnerabilities older than SLA
explanation: KRIs measure risk exposure (count of overdue critical vulnerabilities indicates rising risk). KPIs measure performance (mean time to patch, tickets closed, response time). The exam tests this distinction; many candidates conflate them.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the PRIMARY benefit of using INDEPENDENT (third-party) auditors?
choices: Independence reduces conflict of interest and increases reliance for relying parties
explanation: Independent third parties have no operational stake — their findings carry weight with regulators, customers, and boards. Internal audit complements but does not replace external. Cost and speed are not the primary rationale.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which type of testing sends malformed or unexpected input to find input-handling vulnerabilities?
explanation: Fuzzing (mutation- or generation-based) feeds malformed inputs to surface crashes, memory errors, and parser bugs. Compliance scanning verifies config; synthetic transactions are availability tests; capacity testing measures throughput.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which test-coverage metric is MOST useful for measuring the depth of an automated test suite?
explanation: Coverage metrics (statement, branch, MC/DC for safety-critical) measure how thoroughly tests exercise the code. LOC, compile time, and file count are not coverage measurements. The exam favors statement/branch coverage as the standard answer.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the FIRST step an auditor should take before evaluating controls?
choices: Understand the audit scope, criteria, and obtain audit authority
explanation: Auditors first establish scope, criteria (frameworks/standards being measured against), and authority (engagement letter). Without scope/criteria, findings have no anchor. Vulnerability scans are a tool, not the first step. Comparison shopping is irrelevant.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the BEST description of a 'compensating control' in audit terms?
choices: An alternate control that achieves the security objective when the prescribed control is not feasible
A control added after a breach
explanation: Compensating controls satisfy the SAME objective by alternate means — for example, network segmentation when patching legacy systems is impossible. PCI-DSS explicitly allows compensating controls with documented justification. The other choices are wrong.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: What is the PRIMARY value of a SIEM beyond raw log aggregation?
choices: Correlation of events across sources to detect multi-stage attacks and produce alerts
explanation: SIEM correlates across diverse sources to surface attack patterns invisible in any single log (e.g., login from country A, then sudden privilege grant, then data exfil to country B). Storage and replacement of EDR/firewalls are wrong.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the PRIMARY benefit of a continuous security monitoring program?
choices: Eliminates the need for periodic audits
Surfaces deviations and incidents in near real-time, reducing time-to-detect
explanation: Continuous monitoring shrinks the dwell-time window — the longer an attacker is undetected, the higher the impact. Periodic audits and manual review remain valuable; SIEM is often a continuous monitoring component, not a replacement.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which penetration testing phase typically includes Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) and active reconnaissance?
explanation: Discovery encompasses passive (OSINT, public records) and active (port scans, banner grabs, DNS enumeration) reconnaissance. Planning sets scope and rules; Attack exploits findings; Reporting communicates outcomes.

web_sources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

stem: Why is a sandbox or non-production environment STRONGLY preferred for destructive penetration tests?
choices: Production tests can cause outages and damage data; non-prod isolates risk to test data
explanation: Destructive testing in production risks outages, data corruption, and customer impact. Non-prod isolates exposure. Some controls (resilience, DR) MUST eventually be tested in production-like environments — but with care. Choices A, C, D are wrong.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which best describes 'purple team' activity?
choices: Defenders and attackers competing in isolation
Collaborative engagement where red-team techniques are shared with blue team to improve detection and response
explanation: Purple teaming bridges red (offensive) and blue (defensive) teams to translate attacker techniques into detection and response improvements. Choice A describes traditional red/blue exercises. Audits and tooling are unrelated.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Breach and Attack Simulation (BAS) tools provide which PRIMARY value?
choices: Continuous, automated execution of attacker techniques to validate detection and prevention controls
explanation: BAS platforms automate playbook execution against the production stack so detection coverage can be measured continuously. They complement, not replace, pen testing and SOC. Compliance reporting is incidental.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which log-management practice BEST defends log integrity from a compromised host?
choices: Store logs only on the host
Forward logs to a centralised SIEM/log server in real-time and protect with WORM or hash-chain
Email logs to a personal account
explanation: Real-time forwarding to a separate, hardened, write-once or hash-chained store survives host compromise. Local-only logs can be tampered. Email and compression-delete are not security strategies.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Why is using PRODUCTION data in test environments a security and privacy concern?
choices: Test environments often have weaker controls, increasing exposure of real PII; under GDPR, processing must have lawful basis
explanation: Test environments commonly skip MFA, PAM, encryption, etc. — moving real production data there expands the breach surface. GDPR Article 5 (purpose limitation, minimisation) generally rules out using prod data for testing without de-identification. Synthesise or mask data instead.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which testing practice is MOST appropriate for verifying privacy controls?
choices: Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) and DPIA review with control sampling
explanation: PIAs/DPIAs evaluate processing activities against privacy principles, sampling controls (notice, consent, retention, access, etc.). Pen tests and DAST find technical vulnerabilities, not privacy compliance. Surveys gauge perception, not control effectiveness.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the MOST important content of a penetration-test report?
choices: Findings prioritised by risk, with reproduction steps and concrete remediation guidance
A list of all tools used
explanation: Manager-mindset: deliver actionable findings ranked by business risk with clear remediation. Tools used belong in methodology; opinions add little; cover design is irrelevant. The report is the product.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the BEST evidence to demonstrate that a control is OPERATING effectively?
choices: Sampled artefacts (tickets, logs, attestations) showing the control fired as designed over a period
explanation: Auditors require evidence of operating effectiveness — sampled records over a period prove the control consistently performed. Policy alone shows design intent; vendor brochures and email confirmations are weak audit artefacts.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which scoring system is the WIDELY-ADOPTED standard for prioritising vulnerabilities?
explanation: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System, currently v4.0) provides numeric severity (0-10) with base, temporal, environmental metrics. CVE = identifier; CWE = weakness taxonomy; CCE = configuration enumeration. CVSS is the prioritisation tool.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which framework provides a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques used to inform detection engineering?
explanation: MITRE ATT&CK catalogues real-world tactics (TA), techniques (T), and procedures used by threat actors — the standard reference for detection engineering and adversary emulation. The other options serve different purposes.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the BEST policy for retention of security audit logs?
choices: Retain per regulatory and business requirements (often 1-7 years), with legal-hold capability
Retain only if a breach occurred
explanation: Retention policy reflects legal/regulatory requirements (e.g., HIPAA 6 years, PCI-DSS 1 year minimum) plus operational/forensic need. 'Forever' is unsustainable and may violate minimisation principles. Weekly deletion eliminates forensic capability.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: An organisation reports SOC 2 Type II findings to its customer. Which type of opinion is MOST favourable?
explanation: An unqualified (clean) opinion means controls operated effectively. Qualified flags one or more issues. Adverse means controls did NOT operate effectively. Disclaimer means the auditor could not form an opinion. Customers strongly prefer unqualified.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the BEST description of forensic readiness?
choices: Pre-incident planning, log retention, evidence-handling procedures, and trained personnel ready to support investigations
explanation: Forensic readiness is proactive — pre-arranged tooling, retention, chain-of-custody procedures, and trained staff so investigations can begin without scrambling. Reactive hiring is too late. Indefinite retention is unsustainable; disabled logging defeats forensics.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Why is 100% code coverage a NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT condition for software assurance?
choices: 100% coverage means every line ran but does not prove every CONDITION/path was tested or that assertions were correct
explanation: Coverage proves execution, not correctness — branches, edge cases, security assertions, and threat-model coverage matter beyond line coverage. Manager-mindset: combine coverage with mutation testing, threat-model alignment, and review.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which control BEST defends against a privileged user altering their own audit trail?
choices: Centralised, write-once log forwarding to a system the privileged user cannot administer
Audit logs only on the host
explanation: Separation of duties for log management — privileged users on the source system cannot administer the log destination. Choices A, C, D allow tampering. The exam often tests this principle.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the BEST description of regression testing?
choices: Re-running tests after a change to ensure existing functionality still works
explanation: Regression testing verifies that recent changes have not broken previously working features. Mature CI/CD pipelines run regression suites on every change. The other choices describe other test types.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which type of IR exercise involves discussion-based walk-through with no system changes?
explanation: Tabletop exercises are discussion-based scenarios — low cost, high educational value. Functional/parallel exercises perform actual recovery procedures in test or alongside production. Full-interruption shifts to DR. CTFs are skill competitions.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which assurance method provides the HIGHEST confidence that controls operate effectively over time?
explanation: Independent Type II audits evaluate operating effectiveness over a period — the gold standard for relying parties. Self-attestation is weak. Informal reviews lack rigor. Whitepapers are not assurance.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the BEST description of threat hunting?
choices: Proactive, hypothesis-driven search for adversaries that may have evaded existing detections
explanation: Threat hunting starts from hypotheses (often informed by ATT&CK or threat intel) and queries data for indicators that predefined detections missed. It complements alerting, not replaces it. The other choices describe different activities.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which technique evaluates the security of THIRD-PARTY software components used in an application?
explanation: SCA tools (e.g., dependency scanning) analyse the bill of materials for known vulnerabilities (CVEs in libraries) and license issues. SAST analyses first-party source. DAST is dynamic. Fuzzing tests inputs. Modern SDLC includes SCA gating in CI/CD.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the BEST defensive coding practice against SQL injection?
explanation: Parameterised queries treat input as DATA, not code — making injection structurally impossible. Client-side escape is bypassable. Careful string concatenation is fragile. Hashing destroys legitimate query content. CWE-89 is the canonical SQLi reference.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Which is the BEST indicator of program maturity according to CMM-style models?
choices: Documented, repeatable, measured processes that drive continuous improvement
explanation: Maturity reflects process — defined, measured, optimised. Audit pass rate is a downstream outcome. Headcount and tool spend are inputs, not maturity measures. CMMI levels 1-5 progress from Initial to Optimising.

web_sources.title: DestCert: CISSP Domain 6 — Security Assessment & Testing

stem: Per NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2, what is the FIRST phase of incident response?
explanation: NIST 800-61 Rev 2 phases: Preparation → Detection & Analysis → Containment, Eradication & Recovery → Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned). Preparation includes building the team, tools, and procedures so the rest of the lifecycle is feasible. Rev 3 (2025) restructures around four ongoing functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect-Respond-Recover.

choices: Containment to limit further encryption and lateral spread
Detailed forensic imaging of every affected disk
explanation: Containment limits further damage — must come before exhaustive evidence collection or external communications. Lessons learned is the LAST phase. Imaging is part of investigation but not the immediate priority while encryption spreads. Press releases come after legal/PR coordination.

web_sources.title: K Logix: Navigating IR — NIST 800-61 Containment, Eradication, Recovery

stem: Which is the BEST description of 'eradication' in the IR lifecycle?
choices: Removing the cause (malware, attacker access, vulnerable configurations) so the threat cannot return
explanation: Eradication removes the root cause — malware artefacts, attacker accounts, vulnerable configurations, persistence mechanisms. Recovery (next phase) restores services. Deleting logs is forbidden. Notifications happen alongside.

web_sources.title: K Logix: Navigating IR — NIST 800-61 Containment, Eradication, Recovery

choices: Documenting lessons learned and updating playbooks, controls, and detection logic
Closing tickets without writing them up
Archiving evidence and forgetting the incident
explanation: Lessons learned must translate into changes (control gaps closed, detections added, training updated). Choices A, C, D produce no improvement. NIST 800-61 frames this as 'continuous improvement', explicit in Rev 3.
